paper_title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Building agents that can anticipate the consequences of their actions is long-standing goal of artificial intelligence. World models pursue this goal by predicting how an environment evolves, allowing agents to evaluate possible behaviors before acting (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018). Early visual world models operate in pixel space (Finn et al., 2016; Finn & Levine, 2017), but reconstructing every pixel requires modeling details that may be unpredictable. Latent world models instead predict action-conditioned changes in learned representations (Hafner et al., 2019; 2020) without rendering pixels. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide promising foundation for this approach. Typically, JEPAs learn to predict masked image/video representations from visible context (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024). DINO-WM predicts representations changing from offline interactions (Zhou et al., 2025), while V-JEPA 2-AC post-trains an action-conditioned predictor for planning

sections.content: (Assran et al., 2025). Recent work further improves representation density and temporal consistency (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026), or adapts the model online (Wang et al., 2026). Parallel studies diagnose structural degradation and over-dispersed patch semantics in dense self-supervised representations, and develop structure-aware selection or semantic concentration to improve dense transfer (Dai et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2026). For video representations, T-CoRe reduces temporal sampling uncertainty using two-sided temporal correspondence, while Co-Settle studies the trade-off between intra-video consistency and inter-video separability during image-to-video transfer (Liu et al., 2025; 2026). Despite this progress, we argue that dense patch representations might not be ideal for downstream dynamics learning and planning for three reasons: 1) An objects information is distributed across patches, leaving its structure implicit. Each task-specific predictor must recover this structure, model interactions, and decode the result back into patches. The object organization encoded during pretraining is not exposed as reusable interface. 2) predictor needs relevant and diverse context to balance local and global views of dynamics. Yet patch-based history is highly redundant, making transitions expensive to store and their relevance costly to compute. 3) Patch representations form dense spatial grids without explicit entity correspondence or transport structure. Existing methods therefore compare predicted and goal grids with pointwise ℓ1 or ℓ2 distance (Zhou et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025). When their supports are largely disjoint, these losses can become insensitive to spatial displacement and rank progress poorly. We therefore propose Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which turns dense patches into reusable object-structured interface. task-agnostic decomposition module addresses problem 1) by factorizing the dense feature field into stable semantic slots (Locatello et al., 2020; Seitzer et al., 2023; Nam et al., 2026) and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen for downstream tasks, it preserves the original feature field through reconstruction while exposing its object organization. For problem 2), the temporal stability of slots allows visual history to be stored and reused as compact masks rather than high-dimensional patch representations. Inspired by memory-based Video Object Segmentation (Oh et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2024), our proposed Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) uses statistics of masks associated with the same slots to assess relevance to the current query and retrieve relevant and diverse, potentially non-contiguous transitions. We further design two branches that separate slot-specific dynamics from inter-slot interaction dynamics, reducing the burden on dynamics learning. Finally, problem 3) motivates our Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) loss for planning. Using the temporal correspondence of slots, it replaces pointwise comparison between predicted and goal patch representations with transport between their aligned masks. Moving mask mass across space provides smooth planning signal that remains informative over long displacements. Slot decomposition turns perception-oriented patch field into reusable interface for prediction, memory maintenance, and goal evaluation. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, slotreconstructed features retain most of the semantic information. Across six planar tasks and four Robotic Arm Planning tasks from the REALM-JEPA dataset, Slot-JEPA improves goal-conditioned planning. The contributions are: We introduce Slot-JEPA, which compresses patch representations into shared semantic slots and time-varying masks, separating reusable visual organization from task-specific dynamics and easing predictor learning. We develop TMP to retrieve relevant, non-contiguous transitions from memory instead of relying only on continuous recent-history window. We predict action effects in mask space and use UOT for goal evaluation, providing signal better aligned with spatial progress when ℓ1/ℓ2 losses become insensitive to displacement.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Slot-JEPA connects four lines of work that are often studied separately: joint-embedding representation prediction, object-centric decomposition and dynamics, memory-based video segmentation, and optimal transport. Together, they motivate its slot-and-mask state, transition memory, and spatial planning objective.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: 2.1 JOINT-EMBEDDING PREDICTIVE WORLD MODELS Joint-embedding methods predict target representations rather than reconstructing raw observations, allowing the learned state to retain predictable semantic structure while discarding some pixellevel detail. I-JEPA introduces this principle for masked image regions, and V-JEPA extends it to spatiotemporal video representations (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024). Dense self-supervised features from DINO and DINOv2 provide another strong latent target for spatial prediction (Caron et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2024). Recent work identifies structural degradation over the course of self-supervised training and over-dispersion of semantically related patches, then addresses these issues through structure-aware model selection or explicit semantic concentration (Dai et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2026). In video self-supervision, T-CoRe uses frames on both sides of the prediction target to reduce temporal sampling uncertainty, while Co-Settle studies image-to-video transfer as balance between within-video temporal consistency and cross-video semantic separability (Liu et al., 2025; 2026). These methods primarily concern how useful visual representation is learned. second line of work turns representation prediction into an action-conditioned world model. DINO-WM predicts future DINOv2 patch features from offline interaction trajectories and plans by comparing imagined features with goal features (Zhou et al., 2025). V-JEPA 2-AC post-trains frame-causal, action-conditioned predictor for robot planning, and V-JEPA 2.1 improves the spatial density and temporal consistency of the underlying video features (Assran et al., 2025; Mur-Labadia et al., 2026). Subsequent studies isolate the effects of representation, predictive objective, and planner design (Terver et al., 2026); AdaJEPA adapts the encoder and predictor online from newly observed transitions (Wang et al., 2026); and LeWorldModel investigates stable end-to-end training of JEPA world models from pixels (Maes et al., 2026). Slot-JEPA is complementary to these advances: rather than replacing joint-embedding pretraining, it introduces structured slot-and-mask interface between pretrained dense encoder and action dynamics, together with spatial objective for prediction and planning. 2.2 OBJECT-CENTRIC REPRESENTATION AND DYNAMICS Slot Attention maps set of visual features to small collection of exchangeable components through competition for input tokens (Locatello et al., 2020). Subsequent methods extend this idea from individual images to video. SIMONe separates temporally abstracted object latents from per-pixel mixture assignments (Kabra et al., 2021); SAVi and SAVi++ use temporally propagated slots to support object tracking in synthetic and real videos (Kipf et al., 2022; Elsayed et al., 2022); and SlotFormer learns dynamics over slot sequences for video prediction and planning (Wu et al., 2023). DINOSAUR shows that reconstructing pretrained self-supervised features, rather than RGB pixels, can induce object-centric components in real images (Seitzer et al., 2023). This last observation is especially relevant to our goal of reorganizing pretrained feature field without discarding its semantic information. Object-centric prediction commonly updates the full latent content of every slot at each time step. Causal-JEPA, the closest joint-embedding counterpart, applies masked and future prediction to object-centric latents (Nam et al., 2026); Better Slots, Better Worlds studies how the quality of these latents affects prediction, planning, and robustness (Nazirjonov et al., 2026). In contrast, Slot-JEPA holds reference-derived semantic slot bank fixed within prediction context and predicts its spatial masks. As in unsupervised slot learning generally, these slots are object-centric components rather than guaranteed physical-instance segmentations. 2.3 MEMORY-BASED VOS AND TRANSITION MEMORY Semi-supervised Video Object Segmentation (VOS) must preserve the identity of target while its appearance and location change. Early propagation methods predict the next mask from an initial annotation and recent frames or masks (Perazzi et al., 2017; Oh et al., 2018). Space-Time Memory Networks instead store past imagemask pairs and let the current query read from them (Oh et al., 2019). XMem separates working, long-term, and sensory memories for long videos, while adaptive memory methods retain frames according to their utility rather than keeping every observation (Cheng & Schwing, 2022; Pourganjalikhan & Poullis, 2022). Cutie introduces object-level memory reading, and SAM 2 develops streaming memory architecture for promptable segmentation (Cheng et al.,

sections.title: 2.4 UNBALANCED OPTIMAL TRANSPORT FOR VISUAL CORRESPONDENCE AND CONTROL
sections.content: Pointwise distances compare features or masks only at matching grid locations. They can therefore provide little information about how far mass should move when predicted and target supports do not overlap. Optimal transport instead compares nonnegative spatial measures under ground cost, explicitly charging for displacement between source and target locations. Entropic regularization makes the problem amenable to efficient Sinkhorn scaling (Cuturi, 2013). Unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) further relaxes exact marginal matching by assigning finite penalty to the creation or removal of mass (Chizat et al., 2018b;a). This relaxation is appropriate for visual masks, whose total mass can change with occlusion, viewpoint, scale, or imperfect decomposition. Slot-JEPA applies UOT between masks with the same slot index, using their shared correspondence to preserve semantic grouping. UOT complements pointwise and reconstruction losses during training and supplies displacement-aware goal cost during planning; its ground cost can additionally incorporate obstacle geometry in planar environments.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP We conduct experiments around four questions: 1) Does the slot decomposition preserve the semantic information (Sec. 4.2)? 2) How well does Slot-JEPA perform on visual planning in controlled planar environments (Sec. 4.3)? 3) Does the framework generalize to Robotic Arm Planning (Sec. 4.4)? 4) How does each component contribute to performance (Sec. 4.5)? Representation pretraining. Starting from V-JEPA 2.1 encoder (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026), we pretrain the slot decomposition module and TMP on Kinetics-400 videos (Kay et al., 2017) using inverse transition encoders. We freeze the pretrained visual encoder and slot decomposition module for downstream tasks. The full pretraining setup is given in Appendix B.1. 4.2 PRESERVATION OF SEMANTIC INFORMATION For each image or video frame, the frozen visual encoder and the slot decomposition module jointly provide patch representation for downstream visual understanding tasks. We evaluate linear semantic segmentation on COCOStuff-27 (Caesar et al., 2018), ADE20K (Zhou et al., 2017), and PASCAL VOC (Everingham et al., 2010) to measure category-level structure; monocular depth estimation on NYUv2 (Silberman et al., 2012) and KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012), plus NYUv2-to-SUNRGBD transfer (Song et al., 2015) without adaptation; and VOS on DAVIS-2017 (Pont-Tuset et al., 2017) using zero-shot label propagation. The evaluation settings are detailed in Appendix B.2. Results in Tab. 1 support two conclusions: 1) Slot decomposition preserves the main task-relevant semantics under strong compression. With = 16, the factorized slot representation contains only about 2.5% as many scalars as the dense patch field, yet the slot-reconstructed representation retains the semantic information needed across segmentation, depth, and VOS. 2) Slot reconstruction makes the patch representation more object-aware. We evaluate three in-distribution (ID) tasks and their out-of-distribution (OOD) variants. The ID tasks use the same layouts and object shapes during training and testing, whereas the OOD variants use previously unseen layouts or object shapes. In TwoRoom (also called Wall in prior work) and Maze (Zhou et al., 2025), point agent passes through doorway and ball navigates U-shaped corridor, respectively. Both use position and velocity as rt, while at specifies velocity in TwoRoom and force in Maze. In PushT (Florence et al., 2022; Chi et al., 2025), pusher moves T-shaped object and itself to their target poses; rt is the pusher state and at is relative target tracked by PD controller. The OOD variants TwoRoomR and MazeR randomize obstacle layouts, while PushObj changes the object shape. Each task provides an initial image v0 and visual goal vg. For comparison, we report DINO-WM baselines that additionally use the low-dimensional goal state for planning in TwoRoom and PushT. We evaluate 50 cases per environment using MPC (Rawlings et al., 2026) with CEM (de Boer et al., 2005). See Appendix B.3 for more details. Main results. Tab. 2 reports success rates and indicates whether goal-state input is used. We draw two conclusions: 1) Slot-JEPA improves visual planning in both ID and OOD environments. Using only visual goal, it succeeds in 100%, 100%, and 92% of ID cases and 90%, 96%, and 58% of OOD cases. It also outperforms every baseline that receives the low-dimensional goal state in all four environments where goal-state results are available. 2) Slot masks and UOT cost provide planning signal aligned with progress. As shown in Fig. 2, the obstacle-aware UOT loss changes gradually even far from the goal, which provides smoother landscape compared to ℓ1 losses. sections.title: 5 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Slot decomposition is trained without instance or part annotations, using feature reconstruction rather than physical identity as its objective. Its masks support planning, but one slot may merge multiple objects or split one object, so consistent instanceor part-level decomposition is not guaranteed. This can limit reasoning about specific components and contact points. TMP builds memory from observed transitions and retrieves context using fixed state and mask cues. These cues may miss contact or appearance changes and select redundant examples. Better memory construction and retrieval criteria that balance relevance with diversity remain open problems.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced Slot-JEPA, which factorizes dense visual representations into stable object-structured slots and time-varying spatial masks for action-conditioned prediction. This structure enables UOT planning loss that is better aligned with spatial progress when pointwise losses provide weak guidance. TMP further draws on relevant transitions beyond short contiguous history. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, mixtures of encoder and slot-reconstructed features remain transferable, while six planar environments and four Robotic Arm Planning tasks in the REALMJEPA dataset show improved planning success, especially on the more complex manipulation tasks. These results show the value of combining structured mask prediction, spatially informed goal costs, and transition memory for visual planning.

sections.title: A ADDITIONAL METHOD DETAILS
sections.content: This appendix gives the architecture and procedures shared by pretraining and all downstream tasks. Environment-specific slot and memory initialization, UOT settings, and planning procedures are reported in Appendix B. A.1 COMPLETE SLOT DECOMPOSITION Reference features and initialization. During pretraining, the reference set consists only of the observed/context frames in the sampled clip; none of the target frames to be predicted are used to construct the slots. We encode these frames once and partition their patch features into non-overlapping windows spanning 4 4 spatial patches. Within each window, four input patch tokens at evenly spaced valid positions initialize four local slots. This feature-dependent initialization avoids introducing separate learned slot template while retaining spatial diversity. Local-to-global Slot Attention. Each local window is processed by three Slot Attention iterations. In every iteration, layer-normalized slots form queries and layer-normalized patch tokens form keys and values. Attention is normalized first across the competing slots and then across the input tokens assigned to each slot. The resulting weighted value is passed through GRU update followed by residual two-layer MLP, as formalized in Sec. 3.2. We pool the local slots from all windows and select = 16 of them by farthest-point sampling (FPS) in feature space. FPS starts from valid local slot and repeatedly chooses the slot with the largest distance to its nearest selected slot. The selected features initialize second, global Slot Attention module, which applies the same three-step iterative update to the pooled local-slot candidates and produces the shared slot bank S. The complete local-to-global extraction and mask-decoding network is shown in Fig. 7. Mask decoding and optimization. The mask decoder first projects patch features and slots to width 128. Two decoder blocks alternately update the patch queries by cross-attending to the fixed slot bank and by applying self-attention among patches. For every patchslot pair, an MLP receives the concatenated decoded patch feature and slot feature and produces an assignment logit. softmax across the slots yields , and the mask-weighted slot sum reconstructs the original dense representation as in Eq. (1). We jointly optimize the local and global Slot Attention modules and the mask decoder with the feature-reconstruction and slot-orthogonality terms in Sec. 3.2. The same extracted slot bank is held fixed when decoding the observed, predicted, and goal frames of one environment. The environment-specific choice of inference reference frames and the slot-refresh policy are given in Appendix B. A.2 PREDICTOR ARCHITECTURE, PRETRAINING, AND MEMORY Predictor architecture. Fig. 8 shows the layer-level architecture of the two TMP branches. TMP uses branch-specific contextquery stacks. The reconstructed-feature branch has 12 blocks of width 192 with three attention heads. The mask branch applies separate object-wise predictors at three spatial scales, each with four blocks. Their (spatial size, width, heads) configurations are (16, 48, 3), (12, 96, 3), and (6, 196, 4). The current and future fields are concatenated channel-wise at each scale; the unavailable future query field is replaced by learned tokens. After attention, we retain only the query positions associated with those future tokens, upsample the three outputs, and concatenate them to form mask t+1 . The shared feature branch uses the same contextquery organization on the reconstructed feature field and masks to model interactions across slots. Its output is fused with every object-wise mask feature before the slot-wise softmax. These dimensions are fixed in comparisons with the sequential-predictor ablation unless stated otherwise. Bidirectional pretraining contexts. Each pretraining sample contains seven frames: four observed/context frames and three held-out target frames. We construct both directions from every clip. In the forward case, the first four frames predict the last three; in the backward case, the last four predict the first three. Thus the predictor learns relation between observed transitions and query transition without relying on fixed chronological direction. The observed transitions from the same sampled clip directly form the training context, so pretraining neither retrieves from nor maintains persistent memory bank.

B.1 PRETRAINING Initialization and data. We initialize the visual encoder from the released distilled V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-B/16 checkpoint (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026). This 80M-parameter encoder is distilled from the 2Bparameter V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-G teacher on VisionMix-163M, which combines LVD-142M images with videos from SSv2, Kinetics, HowTo100M, and YT-1B. We then pretrain Slot-JEPA on the training split of Kinetics-400 (Kay et al., 2017), which contains roughly 240,000 clips. The complete dataset contains 306,245 clips from 400 human-action classes. Each clip lasts approximately 10 seconds and comes from distinct YouTube video. Its content spans individual actions such as drawing and drinking, personperson interactions such as hugging and shaking hands, and personobject
